paragraphs: Having examined the makeup of the House of Representatives, and answered those objections against it that seemed to deserve notice, I turn next to the Senate. This part of the government may be considered under five heads: I. The qualifications of senators; II. Their appointment by the State legislatures; III. The equality of representation in the Senate; IV. The number of senators and the term for which they are to be elected; V. The powers vested in the Senate.

I. The qualifications proposed for senators differ from those of representatives in requiring greater age and a longer period of citizenship. A senator must be at least thirty years old, while a representative must be twenty-five. The senator must also have been a citizen for nine years, where seven are required of the representative. The reason for these distinctions lies in the nature of the senatorial trust. That trust calls for a greater range of information and a steadier character, and so calls for a senator who has reached the time of life most likely to supply these qualities. It also involves a direct part in dealings with foreign nations, and so ought to be exercised only by those who have been thoroughly weaned from the prejudices and habits that come with foreign birth and education. The term of nine years seems a prudent middle course. At one extreme is a total exclusion of adopted citizens, whose merits and talents may deserve a share of the public confidence. At the other is a hasty and indiscriminate admission of them, which might open a channel for foreign influence in the national councils.

II. It is equally unnecessary to dwell on the appointment of senators by the State legislatures. Of the various ways in which this branch of the government might have been constituted, the one proposed by the Convention is probably the most agreeable to public opinion. It has a double advantage to recommend it. It favors a select appointment, and it gives the State governments such a part in forming the federal government as must secure their authority, and may serve as a convenient link between the two systems.

III. The equality of representation in the Senate is another point that does not call for much discussion, since it was plainly the result of a compromise between the opposing claims of the large and the small States. It may indeed be right that among a people thoroughly merged into one nation, every district should have a PROPORTIONAL share in the government. It may also be right that among independent and sovereign States bound together only by a simple league, the parties, however unequal in size, should have an EQUAL share in the common councils. If both are right, then it does not seem to be without some reason that in a compound republic, which partakes of both the national and the federal character, the government should be founded on a mixture of proportional and equal representation. But it is pointless to test by the standard of theory a part of the Constitution that everyone admits to be the result, not of theory, but "of a spirit of amity, and that mutual deference and concession which the peculiarity of our political situation rendered indispensable." The voice of America, and still more loudly her political situation, calls for a common government with powers equal to its objects. The smaller States are not likely to grant a government founded on principles more agreeable to the wishes of the larger States. The only choice for the larger States, then, lies between the proposed government and one that is still more objectionable. Given this alternative, prudence advises embracing the lesser evil. Instead of fruitlessly anticipating the harms that may follow, we should consider the advantages that may offset the sacrifice.

In that spirit, note that the equal vote given to each State does two things. It is a constitutional acknowledgment of the share of sovereignty that the individual States still retain, and it is a means of preserving that share. On this score the equality ought to be just as acceptable to the large States as to the small, because the large States are equally anxious to guard, by every possible means, against an improper consolidation of the States into one simple republic.

Another advantage that comes from this ingredient in the makeup of the Senate is the additional obstacle it will place against improper acts of legislation. No law or resolution can now be passed without the agreement, first, of a majority of the people, and then of a majority of the States. It must be acknowledged that this complicated check on legislation may in some instances be harmful as well as beneficial. It must also be acknowledged that the special protection it gives the smaller States would be more reasonable if some interests common to them, and distinct from those of the other States, would otherwise be exposed to particular danger. But the larger States will always be able, through their power over the supplies, to defeat any unreasonable use of this prerogative of the lesser States. And the ease and excess of law-making seem to be the diseases to which our governments are most liable. So it is not impossible that this part of the Constitution may prove more convenient in practice than it appears to many in theory.

IV. The number of senators and the duration of their appointment come next to be considered. To form an accurate judgment on both points, it is proper to inquire into the purposes a senate is meant to serve. To determine these, it is necessary to review the problems a republic must suffer for lack of such an institution.

First. It is a misfortune that comes with republican government, though in a smaller degree than with other governments, that those who administer it may forget their obligations to their constituents and prove unfaithful to their important trust. From this point of view, a senate, as a second branch of the legislative assembly, distinct from the first and dividing power with it, must in all cases be a beneficial check on the government. It doubles the security of the people, by requiring the agreement of two distinct bodies in schemes of usurpation or betrayal, where the ambition or corruption of one would otherwise be enough. This precaution rests on such clear principles, and is now so well understood in the United States, that it would be more than superfluous to enlarge on it. I will only remark that the unlikelihood of sinister combinations will be in proportion to the difference in character between the two bodies. It must therefore be wise to distinguish them from each other in every respect consistent with due harmony in all proper measures and with the genuine principles of republican government.

Second. The necessity of a senate is just as clearly shown by the tendency of all single and numerous assemblies to yield to sudden and violent passions, and to be led by factional leaders into intemperate and destructive resolutions. Examples could be cited without number, both from proceedings within the United States and from the history of other nations. But a position that will not be contradicted need not be proved. All that needs to be remarked is that a body meant to correct this weakness ought itself to be free from it, and so ought to be less numerous. It ought, moreover, to have great firmness, and so ought to hold its authority for a considerable length of time.

Third. Another defect that a senate can supply is a lack of due acquaintance with the objects and principles of legislation. An assembly of men drawn for the most part from private pursuits, kept in office for a short time, and led by no lasting motive to spend the intervals between public duties studying the laws, the affairs and the broad interests of their country, cannot, if left wholly to themselves, escape a variety of serious errors in exercising their legislative trust. It may be affirmed, on the best grounds, that no small share of the present troubles of America is to be blamed on the blunders of our governments, and that these have come from the heads rather than the hearts of most of their authors. What indeed are all the repealing, explaining and amending laws that fill and disgrace our voluminous codes, but so many monuments of deficient wisdom? They are so many charges brought by each session against the one before it, and so many warnings to the people of the value of the help that may be expected from a well-constituted senate.

A good government implies two things: first, fidelity to the object of government, which is the happiness of the people; second, knowledge of the means by which that object can best be attained. Some governments are deficient in both of these qualities; most governments are deficient in the first. I do not hesitate to assert that American governments have paid too little attention to the second. The federal Constitution avoids this error. And what deserves particular notice is that it provides for the second in a way that increases the security for the first.

Fourth. The instability in the public councils that comes from a rapid succession of new members, however well qualified they may be, shows in the strongest way the need for some stable institution in the government. Every new election in the States is found to change one half of the representatives. From this change of men must come a change of opinions, and from a change of opinions, a change of measures. But continual change, even of good measures, is inconsistent with every rule of prudence and every prospect of success. The remark holds true in private life, and it becomes both more just and more important in national affairs.
To trace the harmful effects of an unstable government would fill a volume. I will point out only a few, each of which will be seen to be the source of countless others.

In the first place, it forfeits the respect and confidence of other nations, and all the advantages that go with a national character. An individual who is seen to be inconstant in his plans, or perhaps to conduct his affairs with no plan at all, is marked at once by all prudent people as a speedy victim of his own unsteadiness and folly. His more friendly neighbors may pity him, but all will decline to link their fortunes with his, and not a few will seize the chance to make their own fortunes out of his. One nation is to another what one individual is to another, with this melancholy difference perhaps: nations have fewer benevolent feelings than individuals, and so are under fewer restraints from taking undue advantage of each other's indiscretions. Every nation, therefore, whose affairs betray a lack of wisdom and stability may expect to suffer every loss that the more systematic policy of its wiser neighbors can inflict. But the best lesson on this subject is, unhappily, given to America by the example of her own situation. She finds that she is held in no respect by her friends, that she is the derision of her enemies, and that she is a prey to every nation that has an interest in speculating on her fluctuating councils and embarrassed affairs.

The internal effects of an unstable policy are still more calamitous. It poisons the blessing of liberty itself. It will do the people little good that the laws are made by men of their own choice, if the laws are so voluminous that they cannot be read, or so incoherent that they cannot be understood; if they are repealed or revised before they are published, or undergo such incessant changes that no one who knows what the law is today can guess what it will be tomorrow. Law is defined as a rule of action. But how can something be a rule when it is little known and even less fixed?

Public instability has another effect: it gives the shrewd, the enterprising and the moneyed few an unreasonable advantage over the industrious and uninformed mass of the people. Every new regulation of commerce or revenue, or any rule that changes the value of the various kinds of property, offers a fresh harvest to those who watch for the change and can foresee its consequences. It is a harvest they did not raise themselves; it was raised by the toil and care of the great body of their fellow citizens. In such a state of things it may be said with some truth that laws are made for the FEW, not for the MANY.

From another point of view, an unstable government does great injury. The lack of confidence in the public councils discourages every useful undertaking whose success and profit may depend on existing arrangements continuing. What prudent merchant will risk his fortune in any new branch of commerce when he cannot be sure that his plans will not be made unlawful before they can be carried out? What farmer or manufacturer will organize his work around the encouragement given to some particular crop or enterprise, when he can have no assurance that his preparatory labor and outlay will not make him a victim of an inconstant government? In a word, no great improvement or praiseworthy enterprise can go forward that requires the backing of a steady system of national policy.

But the most deplorable effect of all is the loss of attachment and reverence that steals into the hearts of the people toward a political system that shows so many marks of weakness and disappoints so many of their hopes. No government, any more than an individual, will long be respected without being truly respectable, and it cannot be truly respectable without a certain measure of order and stability.
